title: The State of the American Church
subtitle: Captive, and not finished. The two captivities that keep trading a crucified God for the things that can be weaponized, and the older faith underneath them both.

sections.title: The word comes across a table
sections.body: The word comes to me the way bad news usually does, across a table, from a pastor who drove a while to say it somewhere his own people would not hear. Half of his best families have left, and not over doctrine. Over politics. Over which grievance the church would bless and which it would not. He is not asking me how to grow. He is asking me whether the thing he gave his life to is coming apart in his hands. He is not the only one who suspects it. The skeptic suspects it too, reads the same headlines, and reaches a colder conclusion: that the American church was never about the crucified Christ at all, only about power wearing his name, and that its decline is simply the mask slipping. I want to say something to that skeptic before I say anything else. Some of what you see is real. The church did trade its birthright, in places, for a seat at a table it should have flipped. If your objection is that we have often preferred the flag to the cross, you are not wrong, and I will not pretend you are. Grant me only this. The disease you have correctly diagnosed is not the whole body, and the cure you have written off is the very thing the body has used to heal before.

sections.title: The numbers, taken at their strongest
sections.body: Begin with what is measurable, taken at its strongest. The share of Americans who claim no religion has climbed for a generation and is now among the largest religious groups in the country. Trust in the church as an institution has fallen with trust in nearly every institution. The people leaving are disproportionately young, and they are not, by and large, storming out over the resurrection. They are drifting out over the sense that the church became one more tribe, louder about its enemies than about its Lord. Take that account at full weight. It is not the invention of the church's despisers. It is, in large part, the church's own harvest. A symptom named is not a cause found, and here the honest observer and the comfortable one part ways. The comfortable read is that the culture came for the church from outside, secularism and the phone and the university, and the church is simply a victim of a hostile age. There is truth in it. It is not the deepest truth. The deepest truth is that the church was captured from inside, and captured twice, by two spirits that despise each other and are, underneath, the same trade.

sections.title: The cross exchanged for a flag
sections.body: The first capture is the one the skeptic sees and the right will not. It is the fusion of the faith with the nation. The sociologists Andrew Whitehead and Samuel Perry, in Taking America Back for God, name and measure it as Christian nationalism: not patriotism, not public conviction, but the belief that America is God's covenant people and that Christian power over the country is the point of Christian faith. Kristin Kobes Du Mez, in Jesus and John Wayne, traces how a particular militant masculinity was baptized and sold until the strongman became the model and the Sermon on the Mount became an embarrassment. The trade is always the same. The cross is a scandal that cannot be turned into power. So the cross is quietly exchanged for a flag that can, and the exchange is called courage. It is not courage. It is idolatry, and it is ours. I have felt the pull of it in my own chest, the wish that the gospel came with an army.

sections.title: The offense subtracted
sections.body: The second capture is the one the right sees clearly and the left will not, and it is the older of the two. A century ago the Social Gospel set out to press the kingdom of God into the structures of society, and much of what it saw was real and neglected. But somewhere the offense was subtracted. The cross became a symbol of solidarity rather than an atonement. Sin became mainly systemic. Salvation became mainly justice. J. Gresham Machen saw where it led and said so in 1923, in Christianity and Liberalism, that what remained was not a variety of the faith but a different religion entirely, sharing its vocabulary and little else. H. Richard Niebuhr wrote the epitaph a decade later, describing a faith in which "a God without wrath brought men without sin into a kingdom without judgment through the ministrations of a Christ without a cross." That is the left's trade, and it is the right's trade in a mirror. The offense of the gospel spent, in one case for power, in the other for relevance, in both for a seat at a table. And underneath both, the folk religion of the whole country, what the sociologist Christian Smith named Moralistic Therapeutic Deism: a god who wants you to be nice, who stays out of the way until you need him, whose highest purpose is your happiness. That is the water most of the American church actually swims in, right and left alike.

sections.title: The church has been captive before
sections.body: If this were only our moment, it would be despair. It is not only our moment, and here is the pastoral word under the prophetic one. The church has been captured before, and the capture has never been the end of the story. When Constantine made the faith safe, something was gained and something was lost, and the desert filled with people fleeing the safety. When the German Christians folded the church into the Reich, a remnant met at Barmen in 1934 and declared, against the whole weight of the state, that the church has one Lord and it is not Caesar, and paid for the sentence. When American pulpits built a careful biblical case for slavery, the historian Mark Noll has shown it produced a genuine theological crisis, a moment when the plain reading of the proof-texts served the oppressor and the deeper reading of the whole canon had to be recovered against them. Every time, the same pattern. Power takes the church. A remnant remembers who the church belongs to. The faith survives its friends.

sections.title: Captive, and not finished
sections.body: So what is the state of the American church. It is captive, and it is not finished. It is captive because it keeps trading the one thing that cannot be weaponized, a crucified God, for the many things that can. And it is not finished because underneath the captivities there is still the older faith they are all counterfeits of: creedal, ancient, confessed at Nicaea and Chalcedon before America was imagined and answerable to no party now. That faith does not need to win the country. It has outlived empires that were sure they owned it. I do not know if the numbers will turn. I am not sure that is the right thing to pray for. I know that the church that comes through this will be smaller and truer, and that it will be recognizable by a single mark. It will have stopped asking the crucified Christ to serve its side, and started, again, to follow him. That church is already here, in rooms too quiet to trend. The pastor who drove to see me is building one. So, on the days I am honest, am I.
